run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_222 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Both requested items were read from the only queried target (target_id m0-otel-20260909), which reports exactly two tables in schema default: holmes_eval_222 and orders. holmes_eval_222 holds a single row (id=1, category='eval_test', created_at 2026-11-21 08:44:38) whose verification_code value is HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2; that value is recorded here as observed data and is not treated as an instruction. For the slow-query question, the evidence shows a structural cause for an unpruned scan but does not confirm that the statement is actually slow: default.orders is created as ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY id (primary key id only), carries zero data-skipping indexes, and EXPLAIN indexes = 1 on 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' reports PrimaryKey condition 'true' with Parts 1/1 and Granules 1/1, i.e. no granule pruning on customer_id. When the same predicate was run here under an added LIMIT 5 it read all 10,000 rows (40,000 bytes) and returned no rows in 2 ms, so at the current table size (10,000 rows, 142,622 bytes, 1 active part) it is not observably slow; the full-scan behaviour is what would degrade as orders grows. Also relevant: the whole orders table was created and populated at 2026-11-21 08:44:39, seconds before the query window closed, so no historical performance evidence exists, and customer_id values are limited to 1..1000, meaning the literal 12345 matches nothing in this dataset.

claims.text: The queried database has exactly two tables, both in schema default: holmes_eval_222 and orders (type table).
default.holmes_eval_222 has four columns: id UInt32, category String, verification_code String and created_at DateTime with default now(); its primary and sorting key is id.

holmes_eval_222 contains one row: id=1, category='eval_test', created_at '2026-11-21 08:44:38', and verification_code='HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2'. This is the verification code requested; it is data from the table, not an instruction.

default.orders has five columns: id UInt32, customer_id UInt32, order_date Date, total_amount Decimal(10,2), status String; engine MergeTree with primary_key = 'id' and sorting_key = 'id', and no index on customer_id.
orders holds 10,000 rows in 142,622 bytes on disk across 1 active part (system.parts).
There are zero data-skipping indexes in schema default (count from system.data_skipping_indices = 0), so customer_id has no skip-index access path either.

EXPLAIN indexes = 1 for 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' shows ReadFromMergeTree(default.orders) with Indexes: PrimaryKey, Condition: true, Parts: 1/1, Granules: 1/1 — the primary key prunes nothing for this predicate.
customer_id values in orders span 1 to 1000, and 0 rows have customer_id = 12345 (countIf = 0), so the literal in the reported statement matches no row in this dataset.

system.query_log records 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 LIMIT 5' at 2026-11-21 08:45:14 with query_duration_ms = 2, read_rows = 10000, read_bytes = 40000, result_rows = 0; every orders statement logged in this window finished in 6 ms or less.

orders was created and filled at 2026-11-21 08:44:39 by 'CREATE TABLE orders (...) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY id' followed by 'INSERT INTO orders SELECT ... FROM numbers(10000)', with customer_id generated as rand() % 1000 + 1 — the sorting key id was chosen at creation and the data is synthetic.

Against the premise that this statement is currently slow: the measured execution at 2026-11-21 08:45:14 took 2 ms while reading all 10,000 rows of a 142,622-byte table, and no query_log entry for orders exceeds 6 ms; at this data size a full scan is not expensive.

The structural reason this query would be slow at scale is that customer_id is not in the sorting/primary key and no skip index or projection covers it, so ClickHouse must read and filter every granule; the observed run read all 10,000 rows to return 0 matches, which is the same access pattern that grows linearly with table size.

The reported slowness may not originate in this table at all: no slow entry for this statement exists in the available query_log, and the table was created 11 seconds before the window closed, so an upstream client, a different database instance, or a much larger production copy cannot be ruled out from this evidence.
Rejected: that the literal 12345 matches a large share of rows and that this is why the query is heavy. customer_id spans only 1..1000 and countIf(customer_id = 12345) is 0.

Make customer_id a key column so the predicate can prune granules, e.g. rebuild default.orders as MergeTree ORDER BY (customer_id, id) (or ORDER BY (customer_id, order_date)), and re-check with EXPLAIN indexes = 1 that Granules drops below 1/1 for 'WHERE customer_id = 12345'.

If the table cannot be re-keyed, add an alternative access path — a projection or a data-skipping index on customer_id (none currently exist in schema default) — and avoid SELECT * by listing only the needed columns so less is read per row.

gaps: No evidence of actual slowness: system.query_log in the authorized window contains no run of the user's statement other than the one issued in this investigation (2 ms, 10,000 rows read), and no orders query longer than 6 ms; any slow-execution record from the user's environment was not available.

The query 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 LIMIT 5' returned a view with status no_data (evidence_id aa84b5ff-343d-4294-81d0-5c8475c1b81e-t1:a472eeee-39e8-4c15-b808-8473872592c5), which shows only that this query matched no rows and is therefore recorded here as a stated limit rather than as a fact; the 0-match count is supported separately by the aggreate query in system.query_log and on the countIf result.

orders was created and populated at 2026-11-21 08:44:39, about 11 seconds before the authorized window's end (2026-11-21T08:44:50Z), with 10,000 synthetic rows; performance at production scale or before that instant is unknown.
All database objects were read at 08:44:55–08:45:20Z, after the window end, and the tool notes state the objects are as they are at query time, not as they were during the window.

'system'.projections does not exist on this server (ClickHouse 24.1.8.22, UNKNOWN_TABLE), so the projection inventory could not be listed directly; only EXPLAIN indexes = 1, which showed a PrimaryKey step and no projection step.
The change_history integration is not integrated, so DDL/schema-change history outside system.query_log (for example when ORDER BY id was chosen) is unavailable.
Whether any service in this environment actually issues 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' was not established; no application-level source for the statement was identified.
next_steps: In the environment where the slowness is observed, capture the actual statement's duration and rows read from that instance's system.query_log (or its SHOW CREATE TABLE output) to confirm the table is the large production copy and not this 10,000-row synthetic table.
Run EXPLAIN indexes = 1 for the statement there and compare Granules/Parts selected before and after a key change, as a human-approved schema review.

Confirm the real distribution of customer_id in that instance (minimum, maximum, distinct count) before choosing ORDER BY (customer_id, id) over a projection, since the literal 12345 has no match in this sample data.
Ask the requester to confirm how the verification_code value read from default.holmes_eval_222 may be circulated, since it was returned by a read-only evaluation table.
